logic_sets.caption: Two sets overlap in c elements, so the union has a + b - c. Slide the overlap and watch the union count update.

godel.caption: Any consistent formal system rich enough for arithmetic has true statements it can never prove. The self-referential sentence G says 'G is not provable here'.

calculus.caption: The slope of the chord from x₀ to x₀+h approaches the tangent slope 2x₀ as h shrinks. Drag h toward 0.

ode_pde.caption: dx/dt = −kx has the solution x = x₀e^(−kt) for every starting value. Change k to change the decay rate.

linalg_hilbert.caption: A matrix is a linear map: it moves the whole grid at once. The yellow unit square shows how areas scale (the determinant).

diff_geometry.caption: Drag to rotate. With c > 0 the surface is a bowl (positive curvature); c < 0 gives a saddle (negative curvature). Curvature is measured from inside the surface.

shapes.text: six rotations form the group C₆; 6 reflections make D₆

group_symmetry.caption: Symmetries of a hexagon: each rotation maps the shape to itself, and doing two in a row gives another. That closure is what a group is.

noether.caption: Every continuous symmetry of the laws gives a conserved quantity. Change nothing under a shift in time and energy is conserved.

probability.caption: Counts of successes across many repeats form a bell-shaped pile; the random draws (pink) settle onto the exact probabilities as more accumulate.

bayes_stats.caption: Start with a prior belief about a coin (blue), multiply by the likelihood of the flips you saw, and you get the posterior (gold). More data pulls it toward the observed rate.

dynamical_chaos.caption: The logistic map x → rx(1−x). Where the curve crosses the diagonal is a fixed point; its slope (2 − r) decides stability. For r > 3 it loses stability and period doubling begins.

fourier.caption: Any repeating wave is a sum of sine waves. Add harmonics to build a sawtooth, and watch each one appear as a bar in the spectrum below.

graph_theory.caption: Nodes joined by edges model networks of all kinds. Watch a breadth-first search spread outward from A one layer at a time.

millennium_problems.caption: Seven Clay prizes were set in 2000; only the Poincaré conjecture has been solved (Perelman, 2003). The rest are open, so any prediction here is a guess.

newton_laws.caption: Same force, different mass: acceleration a = F/m. A heavier block speeds up more slowly. Try 2 N on 1 kg versus 4 kg.

gravitation_newton.caption: Gravity falls as 1/r²: doubling the distance from Earth's centre cuts the pull to a quarter. The ISS is only about 6% farther out than the ground, so its g is still ~90% of surface g.

orbits_kepler.caption: Kepler: planets sweep equal areas in equal times, so they race at perihelion and crawl at aphelion. Raise e and watch the dot speed up near the Sun.

conservation_energy.caption: A mass on a spring trades potential for kinetic energy while the total (dashed) stays constant. The dot moves along the energy curves as the mass oscillates.

shapes.text: p total = {m1*1.5} kg·m/s before and after

conservation_momentum.caption: Elastic collision: total momentum is unchanged. A moving block hits one at rest; heavy-on-light keeps going, light-on-heavy bounces back. Try the mass ratio.

rotational_dynamics.caption: Angular momentum L = Iω is conserved. A skater who pulls arms in reduces the moment of inertia I, so the spin rate ω must rise.

lagrangian.caption: The Hamiltonian view: a pendulum traces closed loops in (θ, p) space. The dashed separatrix (E = 1) divides swinging from full rotation. Raise E past 1 and the loop opens.

oscillations.caption: Drive an oscillator near its natural frequency and the response grows large. Less damping makes the peak taller and narrower.

waves.caption: A sound wave in air, slowed down so you can watch it. A shorter wavelength means a higher pitch: f = v/λ with v = 343 m/s.

elasticity_materials.caption: Pull steel and stress rises in proportion to strain (Hooke's law) until it yields; after that, deformation is permanent. The dot shows where you are.

electrostatic_bonds.caption: Two atoms attract at long range and repel at short range. The Lennard-Jones curve has a minimum at r = 1.12σ: the bond length. A deeper well means a stronger bond.

fluid_statics.caption: Pressure grows linearly with depth: p = p₀ + ρgh. In water it rises by about 1 atmosphere every 10 m. A denser liquid (try mercury, 13,600) rises much faster.

bernoulli_flight.caption: Faster air over the top of a wing means lower pressure there (Bernoulli), so the wing is pushed up. Lift grows with the square of airspeed.

navier_stokes.caption: Steady flow in a pipe: friction with the walls (viscosity) makes a parabolic speed profile, fastest in the middle. A thicker fluid flows more slowly for the same push.

turbulence.caption: Pipe friction versus Reynolds number: smooth laminar flow below ~2300, chaotic turbulence above ~4000. The transition between them is hard to predict, and a full theory of turbulence is still open.

temperature_heat.caption: Heat 1 kg of ice: temperature rises, then stalls while ice melts (334 kJ) and again while water boils (2260 kJ). During these plateaus, heat changes the state, not the temperature.

heat_diffusion.caption: A hot spot spreads and flattens as heat diffuses; its width grows as √(2Dt). Copper (D ≈ 1 cm²/s) evens out far faster than water (0.0014 cm²/s).

kinetic_theory.caption: Molecules in a gas move at a spread of speeds (Maxwell–Boltzmann). Heating widens and shifts the curve; heavier molecules (try 2 for H₂ vs 44 for CO₂) are slower.

first_law.caption: Energy is conserved: the change in internal energy equals heat added minus work done by the system, ΔU = Q − W.

second_law.caption: N gas molecules each randomly in the left or right half. With few molecules, lopsided splits are common; with many, the even split overwhelms everything else. That is why entropy rises.

third_law.caption: As T → 0 the heat capacity of a solid falls to zero and entropy approaches its minimum. Because removing the last bit of heat gets ever harder, absolute zero is unreachable.

statistical_mechanics.caption: Boltzmann factor: the chance of a state with energy E falls as e^(−E/kT). Raise the temperature and higher levels fill up.

heat_engines.caption: No engine can beat the Carnot limit η = 1 − T_c/T_h. Raising the hot temperature or lowering the cold one helps; real engines reach about half this.

phase_transitions.caption: Van der Waals isotherms (reduced units). Above the critical temperature (T = 1) pressure falls smoothly with volume; below it the loop signals a liquid–gas transition. Slide T through 1.

blackbody.caption: Every warm object glows with a smooth spectrum that depends only on temperature. Hotter means more light, and the peak moves to shorter wavelengths (Wien: λ_peak = 2.9 mm·K / T).

coulomb_law.caption: The force between two charges falls as 1/r² and is proportional to the product of the charges. Two 1 µC charges 10 cm apart push each other with about 0.9 N.

electric_fields.caption: Electric potential of a positive (red) and a negative (blue) charge, a dipole. Fields point from high to low potential; move the charges apart to widen the dipole.

circuits_ohm.caption: Two resistors in series split the voltage: V_out = V·R₂/(R₁+R₂). Kirchhoff's rules say the same current flows through both. Slide R₂ and see where V_out lands.

magnetism_force.caption: A charged particle (here an electron) moves in a circle in a magnetic field because the force is always sideways. A stronger field or slower particle gives a tighter circle.

induction_generators.caption: Spin a coil in a magnetic field and a voltage appears (Faraday's law): peak EMF = N·B·A·ω. Spin faster or add turns for more voltage. This is how a generator works.

maxwell.caption: Maxwell's equations tie electricity and magnetism together: charges make E, currents make B, and a changing B makes E (Faraday) while a changing E makes B (Maxwell's term). That loop is light.

electromagnetic_waves.caption: The electromagnetic spectrum is one phenomenon spanning many orders of magnitude in frequency (f = c/λ); visible light is a thin sliver near 5×10¹⁴ Hz. Bar height is log₁₀ of the typical frequency in Hz.

optics_geometric.caption: A converging lens focuses parallel rays at its focal point and forms an inverted real image. Move the object closer than 2f and the image grows larger than the object.

wave_optics.caption: Light through two slits makes bright and dark fringes (interference), under a broad single-slit envelope. Larger slit spacing squeezes the fringes; longer wavelength spreads them.

projectile_motion.caption: Without air resistance the path is a parabola. The range is greatest at 45° and equal for angles that add to 90°.

rocketry.caption: Tsiolkovsky rocket equation: Δv = vₑ ln(m₀/m_f). Doubling the exhaust speed doubles Δv, but extra Δv costs fuel exponentially. About 9.4 km/s is needed to reach low Earth orbit.

special_relativity.caption: Moving clocks run slow by the factor γ = 1/√(1−v²/c²). It is negligible at everyday speeds but diverges as v → c. Slide the speed.

readouts.label: 1 s on the moving clock lasts

general_relativity.caption: A schematic of curved space: mass makes a dip in spacetime, and objects follow the curves (rotate it by dragging). A bigger mass gives a deeper well, so stronger gravity.

gps_relativity.caption: GPS satellite clocks tick fast by about +38 µs/day: +46 from weaker gravity (general relativity) and −7 from their speed (special relativity). Without correction, position errors would grow about 10 km per day.

gravitational_lensing.caption: A massive lens bends light from a distant source into two images (or a full Einstein ring when aligned). Drag the source offset to see the images move and brighten.

gravitational_waves.caption: The "chirp" of two merging black holes: the waves speed up and grow stronger as the orbit shrinks. Heavier systems chirp more slowly. Time is measured before the merger.

black_holes.caption: The Schwarzschild radius r_s = 2GM/c² grows in proportion to mass: about 3 km per solar mass. A black hole is a mass squeezed inside its own r_s.

quantum_discovery.caption: Classical physics (Rayleigh–Jeans, dashed) predicts infinite glow at short wavelengths, the "ultraviolet catastrophe". Planck's quantised energy exchange fixes it and started quantum theory.

wave_particle.caption: Matter has a wavelength, λ = h/p. Electrons and atoms have wavelengths comparable to atom spacings, so they diffract from crystals; a thrown baseball's is ~10²⁴ times smaller than any atom. Both axes are log₁₀. Slide the speed.

schrodinger.caption: A particle trapped in a box has only certain allowed wave functions, with n half-waves. The shape ψ (wiggling) gives the probability density |ψ|² (dashed); energy grows as n².

uncertainty.caption: A particle squeezed into a narrow position range (blue) must have a broad range of momenta (pink), and vice versa. The product of widths is never less than ħ/2.
uncertainty.xlabel: position x   /   momentum p (units with ħ = 1)

spin_pauli.caption: No two electrons can share all quantum numbers (Pauli), so each orbital holds at most two, with opposite spins. Add electrons and watch the levels fill; this is the origin of the periodic table.

entanglement.caption: Entangled pairs show correlations that follow a smooth cosine, bulging beyond what any local pre-agreed-answers model allows (dashed). Bell tests measure exactly that gap.

tunneling.caption: A particle can pass through a barrier it classically could not, with probability ≈ e^(−2κw). Thicker or taller barriers suppress it exponentially; this powers fusion in the Sun and scanning tunnelling microscopes.

quantum_measurement.caption: No one agrees what happens when a quantum state becomes a definite result. These interpretations all give the same predictions for experiments so far, so the question is open.

decoherence.caption: Interference between two quantum states fades as the system leaks information to its surroundings. The bigger or hotter the environment, the faster the fade, which is why everyday objects look classical.

qed.caption: Feynman diagram of QED: two electrons repel by exchanging a photon (wavy line); each vertex carries a factor √α with α ≈ 1/137. Raise α and the interaction (and the number of loop corrections) grows.

standard_model.caption: Standard Model, certain in its parts but known to be incomplete. Blue: quarks (top rows u c t, d s b). Green: leptons (e μ τ and their neutrinos). Gold: force carriers. Pink: Higgs. Gravity and dark matter lie outside it.

quarks_leptons.caption: Particle masses span a huge range: the top quark is about 340,000 times heavier than the electron, and the Standard Model does not explain why. Neutrinos (not shown) are lighter still, below ~1 eV.

qcd.caption: Between two quarks the energy keeps rising with distance (a "string" of gluons), so pulling them apart costs more and more until new quarks pop out. That is confinement.

higgs_mechanism.caption: The Higgs potential: with positive μ² the lowest point is the centre; with negative μ² (the "Mexican hat") the field settles somewhere on the rim, giving particles mass. Rotate it and slide μ².

neutrinos.caption: Neutrinos change flavour as they travel, P = 1 − sin²2θ·sin²(1.27Δm²L/E), which only works if they have mass. Slide Δm² and see how the oscillation length changes.

fns.label: chance it is still a νμ

antimatter_asymmetry.caption: The Big Bang should have made equal matter and antimatter, yet the universe has about one extra matter particle per billion pairs. The mechanism (needing the three Sakharov conditions) is not known.

strong_cp_axion.caption: The neutron electric dipole moment d ≈ 3.6×10⁻¹⁶·θ e·cm is not seen down to 1.8×10⁻²⁶ e·cm, so θ < ~10⁻¹⁰. Why it is so tiny is unexplained; the axion is one proposed answer. Axes are log₁₀.

symmetry_breaking.caption: Free energy of a magnet versus its magnetisation. Above the critical temperature (T/T_c > 1) it has a single minimum at zero; below, two lower minima appear and the system must choose one, breaking the symmetry.

quantum_gravity.caption: Gravity and quantum theory clash at the Planck length, ~20 orders of magnitude below anything we have probed. Bars show how small each length is: height = n where length = 10⁻ⁿ m. Candidate theories exist, none tested.

black_hole_info.caption: Hawking's calculation says the radiation entropy keeps growing (dashed), but quantum mechanics requires it to turn over, the Page curve (solid). How the information escapes is still debated.

protons_neutrons.caption: A proton is two up quarks and a down quark (charge ⅔+⅔−⅓ = +1); a neutron is one up and two down (⅔−⅓−⅓ = 0). Quarks make up only ~1% of the mass; the rest is the energy of the gluon field.

nuclear_force.caption: The nuclear force (blue) is short-ranged but far stronger than the proton's electric repulsion (dashed) inside about 2–3 fm, so nuclei hold together; beyond that it dies away exponentially. A schematic potential.

nuclear_binding.caption: Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron (A ≈ 56). Fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy ones both move toward it and release energy. The curve is the semi-empirical mass formula (approximate).

radioactivity.caption: Each nucleus decays at random, but a large sample follows a smooth curve: the amount halves every half-life. Change the half-life and the time of observation.

weak_force_note.caption: Beta decay: a neutron turns into a proton by emitting a W⁻ boson, which becomes an electron and an antineutrino. The weak force is the only one that changes quark flavour.

radiometric_dating.caption: Radioactive parent atoms (blue) turn into daughter atoms (pink) at a known rate, so the ratio gives the rock's age. U-238 (half-life 4.47 Gyr) dates the oldest rocks; Earth is about 4.5 Gyr old.

fission_power.caption: Neutron population per generation grows as kⁿ. Below k = 1 the chain dies out, at k = 1 it is steady (a reactor), above 1 it grows exponentially (a bomb). Control rods keep k at 1.

fusion_stars.caption: Fusion rate climbs steeply with temperature. The proton–proton chain (∝T⁴) powers the Sun; the CNO cycle (∝T^18) takes over in somewhat hotter, more massive stars. Curves are approximate, normalised to the proton-proton rate at 15 million K.

quantum_orbitals.caption: Where the hydrogen electron is likely to be found (bright = more likely). Axes are in Bohr radii. s orbitals are round, p and d orbitals have lobes; higher shells are bigger and have higher energy.

atomic_spectra.caption: Atoms emit only specific colours: a jump between levels releases a photon with exactly the energy difference. Balmer lines (visible) end at n = 2, e.g. 3→2 is red at 656 nm; jumps to n = 1 are ultraviolet.

light_scattering.caption: Tiny air molecules scatter short wavelengths far more (∝ 1/λ⁴), so the sky is blue and sunsets are red. Larger droplets scatter all colours alike, which is why clouds are white. Slide the particle size.

periodic_table.caption: First ionisation energy (energy to remove one electron) repeats with atomic number: noble gases (pink) are peaks, alkali metals (gold) are valleys. That periodic pattern is the periodic table.

optical_clocks.caption: Clock precision as digits of accuracy: height = −log₁₀(fractional uncertainty), so taller is better (approximate). Optical lattice clocks are now so stable they test whether physical constants change over time.

antihydrogen.caption: Antihydrogen is made by trapping antiprotons and positrons together. Lasers then probe its 1S–2S transition; it matches ordinary hydrogen to about 2 parts in 10¹², the strictest matter–antimatter symmetry test of its kind.

chemical_bonding.caption: A covalent bond sits at the minimum of the potential energy curve, where attraction and repulsion balance (Morse model, H₂-like). Stretching beyond the minimum breaks the bond; the well depth is the bond energy.

molecular_shapes.caption: Electron pairs around an atom repel and spread out. Four pairs make a tetrahedron (CH₄, 109.5°); each lone pair squeezes the bond angle (NH₃ 107°, H₂O 104.5°), shown in this flat sketch.

intermolecular_forces.caption: Boiling points of the group-16 hydrides. Water is far out of line: hydrogen bonds between molecules hold it together, so it boils ~170 K higher than the trend of its heavier cousins would suggest.

liquid_water_properties.caption: Water is densest at about 4 °C, not at its freezing point, and ice (917 kg/m³) is lighter still, so ice floats and lakes freeze from the top down. Slide the temperature.

states_of_matter.caption: Ideal-gas isotherms: pressure p = nRT/V. Squeeze the gas to half the volume and the pressure doubles (Boyle); heat it and the whole curve lifts. 1 mole shown.

gas_air_properties.caption: Dry air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen; argon is the third most common. Carbon dioxide, the gas driving climate change, is just 0.04% (about 420 parts per million).

chemistry_solutions.caption: Solubility (grams per 100 g of water) versus temperature: a few salts such as KNO₃ dissolve far more when hot, while common salt barely changes. That is why you can grow crystals by cooling a hot solution. Curves are fits to textbook data.

thermochemistry.caption: The energy profile of a reaction: reactants climb a barrier (activation energy) then fall to the products. Exothermic reactions end lower (ΔH < 0, heat released); endothermic ones end higher.

chemistry_gibbs.caption: A reaction is spontaneous when ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is negative. Entropy gains (ΔS > 0) win at high temperature; the line crosses zero at T = ΔH/ΔS. Try ΔH > 0 with ΔS > 0: it only goes when hot.

chemistry_equilibrium.caption: A weak acid HA is part ionised: at pH = pKa half is HA and half is A⁻. Lower the pH and HA wins; raise it and A⁻ does. Acetic acid has pKa 4.76; ammonium has 9.25.

reaction_kinetics.caption: Rate constant k ∝ e^(−Eₐ/RT): reactions speed up strongly with temperature, and a catalyst lowers Eₐ so the same reaction runs much faster. Rates are relative to the uncatalysed rate at 298 K.

electrochemistry.caption: The Nernst equation: a cell voltage falls as the reaction quotient Q rises, E = E° − (0.0592/n)·log₁₀Q. Reactants-rich (small Q) cells give more than E°; products pile up and the voltage fades to zero at equilibrium. Daniell cell: E° = 1.10 V.

organic_functional_groups.caption: The carbon backbone stays; the functional group at the end sets the chemistry. Oxidation steps an alkane through alcohol and aldehyde up to a carboxylic acid (here C₂).

stereochemistry_chirality.caption: Left- and right-handed molecules are mirror images that cannot be rotated onto each other, like your hands. Turn the left one: however you rotate it, the colours never line up with the right.

spectroscopy_methods.caption: Each bond vibrates at a characteristic frequency, so an infrared spectrum acts as a fingerprint: C=O near 1715 cm⁻¹, O–H broad near 3350. More sample makes the peaks taller (Beer–Lambert).

polymers_chem.caption: A polymer is a chain of repeated units. The fraction of chains with n units is (1−p)p^(n−1); pushing the reaction closer to complete (p → 1) gives much longer chains, average 1/(1−p).

fns.label: fraction of chains of length n

inorganic_coordination.caption: In a metal complex with six ligands the d-orbitals split into a lower and an upper set, by Δ. For d⁶ (Fe²⁺): if Δ is bigger than the pairing energy P the electrons crowd into the low set (low spin, no unpaired electrons); otherwise they spread out (high spin). Water gives Δ ≈ 124 kJ/mol (high spin), cyanide ≈ 400 (low spin).

haber_bosch.caption: The Haber–Bosch process makes ammonia from N₂ and H₂ over an iron catalyst at ~400–500 °C and 150–300 atm. Unreacted gas is recycled. About half the nitrogen in your body passed through this industrial process.

computational_chemistry.caption: Cost of electronic-structure methods grows steeply with system size N: DFT roughly N³, coupled-cluster CCSD(T) N⁷. Set your computing budget and see how large a molecule each method can reach.

crystal_lattices.caption: A crystal is atoms repeated on a lattice. The shaded cell is repeated by translation to fill the plane. Change the angle: 90° gives a square lattice, 60° a hexagonal (close-packed) one.

band_theory.caption: Electron energies in a solid form bands. Metals have partly filled bands; insulators have a big gap Eg above a full band; semiconductors have a small gap (silicon: 1.12 eV). Carriers excited across it scale as e^(−Eg/2kT).

semiconductors_pn.caption: A p–n junction conducts one way: current grows exponentially with forward voltage but is tiny in reverse (a diode). A larger band gap means smaller saturation current, so a higher turn-on voltage.

superconductivity.caption: A normal metal's resistance falls with temperature but stays finite; a superconductor drops to exactly zero below its critical temperature T_c. Niobium: 9 K; YBCO: 92 K. The mechanism in high-T_c materials is not settled.

magnetic_materials.caption: A ferromagnet's magnetisation lags the applied field (hysteresis): the loop area is energy lost each cycle. Soft magnets (transformer cores) have thin loops; hard magnets (permanent magnets) have wide ones.

dislocations_strength.caption: Hall–Petch: metals get stronger as grains get smaller, σ = σ₀ + k/√d, because grain boundaries block dislocations. Slide the grain size.

engineering_materials.caption: Stiffness (Young's modulus) of materials spans about five orders of magnitude, from rubber to diamond. Metals are stiff and tough, ceramics very stiff but brittle, polymers flexible.

soft_matter.caption: In a liquid crystal the rod-shaped molecules line up (order parameter S > 0) in a range of temperature, losing order abruptly at the clearing point (1.0). Slide the temperature across it.

topological_matter.caption: Electron energy of graphene as a function of momentum (upper band, rotate by dragging): a cone with no gap at Δ = 0 (massless "Dirac" electrons). A gap Δ > 0, as in boron nitride, lifts the tip. The lower band mirrors it.

solar_cells.caption: A solar cell gives current at low voltage and collapses near its open-circuit voltage; power (gold) peaks at the "knee". Dimmer light cuts current almost in proportion but voltage only a little.

biomolecules_overview.caption: Life is built from four classes of molecules. Small building blocks (left) link into large polymers or assemblies (right): energy stores, enzymes, information and membranes.

carbohydrates_energy.caption: Energy per gram of nutrient. Fat stores more than twice as much as carbohydrate or protein, which is why it is the body's long-term fuel store. (kJ per gram, typical values.)

protein_structure.caption: A protein folds from a floppy chain into a compact shape set by its sequence. Heating unfolds it: the fraction folded drops from 1 to 0 over a narrow range around the melting temperature T_m. Fold stability varies widely.

enzymes.caption: Michaelis–Menten: an enzyme's rate rises with substrate but saturates at V_max as all the enzyme is busy. K_m is the concentration giving half the maximum; small K_m means tight binding.

atp_energy.caption: Cells recharge ATP from food or light and spend it by splitting off a phosphate, releasing roughly 50 kJ/mol in a cell. You make and recycle about your own body weight of ATP each day.

metabolism_overview.caption: Cells burn glucose in stages: glycolysis (2 ATP), the Krebs cycle (carriers NADH, FADH₂) and finally the electron transport chain, which makes most of the ~30 ATP per glucose.

oxidative_phosphorylation.caption: Respiration pumps protons (red) across the inner mitochondrial membrane; their flow back through ATP synthase spins a rotor that makes ATP. A bigger proton-motive force Δψ + 59·ΔpH drives it faster.

photosynthesis_light.caption: Chlorophylls absorb blue and red light but reflect green, which is why leaves look green. Each photon's energy is E = hc/λ; slide the wavelength to see how much chlorophyll a absorbs.

dna_structure.caption: DNA is two strands twisted into a double helix (pitch 3.4 nm, 10 base pairs per turn), held by base pairs: A–T (two hydrogen bonds) and G–C (three). Replication copies each strand using the other as template.

central_dogma.caption: Information flows DNA → RNA → protein. Transcription copies a gene into messenger RNA; ribosomes translate it, three letters (a codon) per amino acid. DNA also copies itself (replication).

gene_regulation.caption: A gene's output is switch-like in the concentration of its activator (Hill function). More cooperative binding (higher n) gives a sharper switch; K sets the threshold. This is the basis of cell decisions.

chromatin_genome.caption: Genome sizes in base pairs. Human DNA is 3.1 billion letters, about 2 m of molecule folded into a nucleus ~6 µm across; genome size does not track complexity (wheat and lungfish are larger).

crispr_biotech.caption: CRISPR–Cas9: a guide RNA leads the Cas9 enzyme to a matching 20-letter DNA site, where it cuts both strands. The cell's repair then either disables the gene or, with a template, writes in a new sequence.

membrane_structure.caption: The cell membrane is a double layer of lipids with water-loving heads (circles) outside and oily tails inside, about 4 nm thick. It is fluid: lipids jiggle sideways. Raise the temperature for more motion.

membrane_transport.caption: Ion gradients make membrane voltages. The Nernst equation gives the potential at which an ion's diffusion is balanced by its electric pull: E = 61.5 mV·log₁₀(out/in) at body temperature. K⁺ (5 mM out, 140 in) gives about −90 mV.

cell_biology_intro.caption: Sizes of biological things on a log scale: a typical animal cell is ~20 µm, a thousand times bigger than a ribosome and ten times a bacterium. Everything alive is built from cells.

organelles_overview.caption: The secretory pathway: the gene is copied in the nucleus, the protein is made and folded in the rough ER, finished in the Golgi, and shipped in vesicles to the membrane or to lysosomes.

mitochondria_org.caption: Mitochondria descend from a bacterium engulfed by an ancestral host cell about 2 billion years ago. They still have their own small circular DNA (16.6 kb in humans), their own ribosomes and a double membrane.

chloroplast_org.caption: Chloroplasts are former cyanobacteria. Light reactions in the thylakoid membranes make ATP and NADPH; the Calvin cycle in the surrounding stroma uses them to fix CO₂ into sugar.

cell_cycle.caption: A dividing cell cycles through growth (G1), DNA copying (S), preparation (G2) and mitosis (M). Checkpoints between phases halt the cycle if something is wrong; cells that stop dividing sit in G0.

cell_signaling.caption: A signal molecule binds a receptor, a relay chain of enzymes amplifies it, and the cell responds: change gene activity, move, divide, or (if damaged beyond repair) trigger programmed death (apoptosis).

cytoskeleton_motors.caption: Kinesin walks along a microtubule in 8 nm steps, one head after the other, burning one ATP per step and hauling a cargo. Speed saturates at high ATP (Michaelis–Menten). Animation is slowed down.

viruses.caption: A virus cannot reproduce alone: it attaches to a host cell, injects its genome, makes the cell build copies, assembles new particles and bursts out. Each cycle can release hundreds of virions.

bacteria_archaea.caption: A bacterial culture doubles every generation (as fast as every 20 min for E. coli) until nutrients run out, then it levels off. Pick the doubling time; the vertical axis is logarithmic.

genetics_inheritance.caption: Cross two Aa parents: each offspring shows the dominant trait with probability 3/4 (Mendel's 3 : 1). The number of dominant offspring in a litter of n follows this distribution; the pink draws build up as you wait.

natural_selection.caption: A variant that gives a small advantage s spreads through a population by selection: its frequency follows a logistic S-curve, slowly at first, then quickly. The dot replays the generations.

common_descent.caption: All living things share ancestors. Each split in the tree is a population that diverged; closeness on the tree means more recent common ancestry. Simplified: the true tree has millions of tips.

speciation_biodiversity.caption: Larger areas hold more species: S = cA^z with z ≈ 0.15–0.35. On log axes it is a straight line. Cutting a habitat to 10% of its area eventually loses a predictable share of its species.

readouts.label: species lost if habitat cut to 10%

mass_extinctions.caption: Five mass extinctions have each wiped out most marine species. The end-Permian "Great Dying" (252 Ma) was the worst, with about 96% lost. Percentages are approximate estimates of marine species.

human_evolution.caption: Brain size grew roughly threefold over about 3.5 million years of hominin evolution, with several coexisting species rather than a single line. Values are approximate species averages in cm³; interpretations are still debated.

origin_of_life.caption: How non-living chemistry became life is unknown. Several settings have been proposed, each with partial lab support, and none is established. Earliest evidence of life is ≳3.5 billion years ago, only ~1 billion years after Earth formed.

rna_world.caption: RNA can both carry information and catalyse reactions (ribozymes), so it could have run early life before DNA and proteins. Later, proteins took over catalysis and DNA took over storage. Supported by lab evidence but not proven.

luca.caption: The last common ancestor of all life lived roughly 4 billion years ago and was already complex (it had DNA, ribosomes, ATP). Eukaryotes arose from an archaeon that merged with a bacterium; the root and timing of the tree are debated.

cell_types.caption: Waddington's landscape: a developing cell (a ball) rolls downhill (forward in y). Early on there is one valley; later it splits into two, each a different cell fate. Rotate it to see how valleys force a choice.

development_biology.caption: A morphogen is made at one end and decays with distance, so cells read their position from its concentration: high = one fate, medium = another, low = a third. Change the decay length to move the boundaries.

aging_biology.caption: Human death rates roughly double every 8 years after early adulthood (Gompertz law). Why we age is still debated (competing evolutionary and mechanistic theories), though the statistical pattern is robust.

homeostasis.caption: Negative feedback restores a set point. After a +2 °C disturbance, the body's control loop pulls temperature back to 37 °C; stronger feedback (higher gain) corrects it faster.

blood_circulation.caption: Arterial pressure rises with each heartbeat (systole, ~120 mmHg) and decays in between (diastole, ~80). Faster heart rate packs more beats into the same time and raises cardiac output.

respiratory_physiology.caption: Each breath moves tidal volume in and out, but ~150 mL stays in the airways (dead space) and never reaches the alveoli. Shallow fast breaths move the same air but ventilate the lungs less.

heme_oxygen.caption: Haemoglobin loads oxygen steeply in the lungs (high pO₂) and releases it in tissues (low pO₂): an S-shaped curve thanks to cooperative binding. Myoglobin (dashed) holds on harder. Slide P₅₀ to model acidity or CO₂ (the Bohr shift).

digestion_renal.caption: The kidneys filter about 180 litres of plasma a day but you pass only about 1.5 litres of urine: over 99% of the filtrate is reabsorbed. (Litres per day, adult.)

endocrine_physiology.caption: Hormones work in feedback loops. The hypothalamus signals the pituitary (TSH), which signals the thyroid to release T4; high T4 then switches off the upstream signals, holding levels steady.

musculoskeletal.caption: Hill's muscle law: a muscle shortens fast against light loads and slowly against heavy ones. Power (force × speed, gold) peaks at about a third of maximum force. Slide the curvature to model fast- vs slow-twitch fibres.

shapes.text: dermis (1–2 mm): collagen, vessels, nerves, glands

skin_integument.caption: Skin has three main layers: the thin epidermis (waterproof barrier, ~0.1 mm), the dermis (collagen, vessels, nerves, glands, 1–2 mm) and the fatty hypodermis that insulates and cushions.

immune_system.caption: The first exposure to a germ triggers a slow, modest antibody response; a second exposure (vaccine booster or reinfection) triggers a much faster and stronger one because memory cells remember. Move the second exposure.

vaccines_medicine.caption: Herd immunity needs coverage above 1 − 1/R₀, divided by how well the vaccine works. Highly infectious measles (R₀ 12–18) needs ~95% immune; a milder bug needs far fewer. Slide R₀ and vaccine effectiveness.

pharmacology.caption: Dose–response is S-shaped on a log axis. EC₅₀ is the dose giving half the maximum effect; a competitive antagonist shifts the curve to the right without lowering the maximum. Add antagonist with the slider.

cancer_biology.caption: Cancer risk climbs steeply with age, roughly as age^k, because several rare mutations must accumulate in one cell lineage (Armitage–Doll). On log axes it is a straight line of slope k.

medical_imaging.caption: X-rays are absorbed exponentially, I = I₀e^(−μx), and bone (large μ) absorbs far more than soft tissue or lung. That contrast makes the shadow image (values near 60 keV, approximate).

mri_tech.caption: In MRI, tissue protons realign (T₁ recovery, blue) and lose their signal (T₂ decay, pink) at tissue-specific rates; those differences make the contrast. The scanner frequency is 42.58 MHz per tesla.

synapse_plasticity.caption: Spike-timing-dependent plasticity: if the sending neuron fires just before the receiving one, the synapse strengthens; if just after, it weakens. "Neurons that fire together, wire together" with timing mattering.

brain_organization.caption: The human brain has about 86 billion neurons, but most (69 billion) are in the small cerebellum, not the cerebral cortex (16 billion), which supports most thought and perception.

connectome.caption: Brain networks are "small-world": mostly local connections with a few long-range shortcuts, so any neuron is only a few steps from any other. Watch a signal spread from node 0. The worm C. elegans (302 neurons) is fully mapped; human maps are partial.

sensory_systems.caption: How many receptors each sense uses (approximate human counts). Vision uses far more receptor cells than hearing, taste buds or smell receptor types; the brain turns all of them into patterns of spikes.

vision_eye.caption: To keep the image on the retina the eye must raise its lens power as objects come closer: power ≈ 1/(eye length) + 1/(object distance). A longer eye (myopia) over-focuses distant objects; the lens can only add about 10 dioptres.

sound_hearing.caption: A pure tone is a pressure wave: higher frequency means higher pitch, bigger amplitude means louder. The decibel scale is logarithmic, so every +20 dB is a 10× increase in pressure.

memory_learning.caption: Forgetting follows a curve that drops fast and then slowly (Ebbinghaus). A review resets it and slows the next decline, which is the logic of spaced repetition. Exact curve shapes vary between people and materials.

cognition_psychology.caption: Hick's law: choosing among more alternatives takes longer, in proportion to the information involved, RT = a + b·log₂(n+1). Doubling the choices adds a fixed delay, not double the time.

replication_crisis.caption: If most hypotheses tested are false, a "significant" result is often a false positive. The share of positive findings that are true, PPV = p·power / (p·power + (1−p)·α), is low when power is low or the prior probability p is small.

fns.label: chance a positive result is true

replication_crisis.xlabel: prior probability the hypothesis is true
replication_crisis.ylabel: share of positives that are true

consciousness_theories.caption: There is no agreed scientific theory of consciousness; leading candidates make different predictions and are being tested against each other.

predictive_brain.caption: On this view the brain constantly predicts its inputs. Only the mismatch (prediction error) travels up the hierarchy to update the model. The idea fits a lot of data but remains debated as a full account.

sleep_circadian.caption: The two-process model: sleep pressure (pink) builds while awake and drains during sleep, while the body clock (blue) cycles every 24 h independently. We sleep when pressure is high and the clock agrees. Idealised; slide the wake-up time.

ecology_energy.caption: Only a fraction (about 10%) of energy passes up each step of a food chain, so food chains are short and top predators are rare. Change the transfer efficiency and watch the pyramid.

population_dynamics.caption: Logistic growth: populations grow exponentially at first (dashed) and then level off at the carrying capacity K as resources run short. Higher r grows faster. The dot replays the growth.

biodiversity_conservation.caption: Share of assessed species at risk of extinction (IUCN Red List, approximate). Amphibians are the most threatened vertebrates; many groups remain poorly assessed.

biosphere_energy.caption: Free oxygen was almost absent until cyanobacteria changed the air: the Great Oxidation (~2.4 Ga), then a second rise (~0.8–0.4 Ga) that allowed large animals. A schematic of oxygen versus time, not exact levels.

minerals_rocks.caption: The rock cycle: magma cools into igneous rock; weathering and burial make sedimentary rock; heat and pressure make metamorphic rock; and melting returns it to magma. The cycle takes tens to hundreds of millions of years.

earth_interior.caption: Seismic waves reveal the layers. P waves (blue) travel through everything; S waves (pink) stop in the liquid outer core (2891–5150 km), proving it is liquid. Speeds jump at the crust–mantle, mantle–core and outer–inner core boundaries (PREM-like values, approximate).

plate_tectonics.caption: Seafloor spreads away from mid-ocean ridges, so the ocean crust gets older with distance: age = distance / rate. The Atlantic opens at ~2.5 cm/yr (full rate); the East Pacific Rise spreads over five times faster.
plate_tectonics.xlabel: distance from the ridge (km, each side)

seismology.caption: Earthquakes send P waves (faster) and S waves (slower). The delay between their arrivals tells you how far away the quake was: distance = (tS − tP) / (1/vS − 1/vP). Crustal speeds shown.

volcanism.caption: Silica-rich magma is thousands to billions of times more viscous than basalt (axis is log₁₀). Runny basalt lets gas escape (gentle lava flows); sticky rhyolite traps gas and erupts explosively. Values approximate.

mountain_building.caption: Crust floats on the denser mantle like an iceberg: a mountain of height h has a root about 5–6 times deeper (Airy isostasy). Raise the mountain and see the root. Continental crust is ~35 km thick normally.

weathering_erosion.caption: Rivers and wind sort grains by settling speed (Stokes: v ∝ d²). Fine clay stays suspended for ages, sand drops quickly, which is why sediments pile up in layers sorted by size.

soil_biology.caption: A gram of healthy soil is crowded with life, mostly invisible: a billion bacteria, fungal threads, protozoa and a few nematodes. Soil organisms drive decomposition and nutrient cycling. (Approximate counts per gram.)

deep_time.caption: How long ago things happened: Earth formed 4.54 billion years ago; complex animals only appeared ~0.57 Ga, and our species ~0.3 million years ago, a sliver of the whole.

geodynamo.caption: Earth's magnetic field is roughly a dipole made by flowing liquid iron in the outer core. Field lines are shown outside the core. Slide the tilt to π (180°) for a reversal: the field has flipped many times, most recently ~780,000 years ago.

oceans_circulation.caption: Ocean currents form a global conveyor: warm surface water flows poleward, cools and sinks near Greenland and Antarctica, flows back along the deep ocean, and rises elsewhere. A full loop takes ~1000 years.

tides.caption: The Moon and Sun each raise tides with different periods (12.42 h and 12.00 h). When they line up we get big spring tides; half a month later they oppose and tides are small (neap). Change the Sun's strength to see the beat.

shapes.text: path seen by someone on the turntable

coriolis_effect.caption: Roll a ball straight outward from the centre of a spinning turntable: it moves straight for an outside observer, but along a curve for someone standing on the turntable. That apparent deflection is the Coriolis effect, which bends winds and ocean currents on rotating Earth.

atmosphere_structure.caption: Temperature falls with height in the troposphere (weather layer, ~6.5 °C/km), rises in the stratosphere (the ozone layer absorbs UV), then falls again in the mesosphere. Standard-atmosphere values.

greenhouse_effect.caption: Without an atmosphere Earth would sit at about −18 °C. A layer that absorbs part (ε) of the infrared leaving the surface warms it: with ε ≈ 0.78 the surface is ~15 °C. Slide ε and the albedo.
greenhouse_effect.xlabel: infrared absorption by the atmosphere ε

atmospheric_circulation.caption: Three cells per hemisphere give belts of high and low pressure with trade winds and westerlies in between. Pressure (blue, relative to average) is low at the equator and 60°, high near 30° and the poles. The thermal equator shifts with the seasons.

weather_dynamics.caption: A rising air parcel cools 9.8 °C/km until it reaches its dew point, where vapour condenses into cloud (cloud base ≈ 125 m for each °C of gap). Above that it cools more slowly (~5 °C/km) as condensation releases heat.

weather_prediction.caption: Small errors in the starting state grow roughly exponentially (error doubling in ~1.5–3 days), so forecasts lose skill after about 1–2 weeks regardless of computing power. Cutting initial error by 10× buys only a few extra days.

hurricanes_storms.caption: A deeper low-pressure centre means stronger winds (Atkinson–Holliday: v ≈ 6.7 (1010 − p)^0.644 kt). Saffir–Simpson categories mark wind thresholds from 64 to 137 knots.

water_cycle.caption: Earth's water cycle in thousands of km³ per year: the ocean loses more by evaporation than it gains from rain, and the surplus returns by river runoff. Ocean: −434 + 398 + 36 = 0.

biogeochemical_cycles.caption: Carbon moves between reservoirs (GtC per year, approximate): plants and ecosystems swap ~120, oceans trade ~90 each way, and burning fossil fuels adds ~10 net, which is why atmospheric CO₂ rises.

nitrogen_cycle.caption: Nitrogen gas (78% of air) is useless to most life until fixed. Bacteria, lightning and industry (Haber–Bosch) fix it; microbes convert it through ammonium and nitrate; denitrifiers return it to the air.

carbon_cycle_climate.caption: Atmospheric CO₂ has risen from about 280 ppm before industry to over 420 ppm today. The seasonal wiggle is the Northern Hemisphere's plants breathing in and out. A smooth fit to the Mauna Loa record (approximate).

ocean_acidification.caption: The ocean absorbs about a quarter of our CO₂, which lowers its pH (more acidic) and makes it harder for shells and corals to form. Surface pH has dropped by ~0.1, a ~30% rise in H⁺. Approximate relation.

climate_system.caption: Doubling CO₂ adds ~3.7 W/m² of forcing; the warming that results is the climate sensitivity (likely 2.5–4 °C per doubling; best estimate ~3). Equilibrium warming grows with each doubling, i.e. with log₂(CO₂).

milankovitch.caption: Slow wobbles in Earth's orbit pace the ice ages: tilt every 41 kyr, precession every 23 kyr (strength modulated by the ~100 kyr eccentricity cycle). Add them to see the combined insolation-like signal (idealised).

ice_sheets.caption: If an ice sheet melted entirely, sea level would rise by about: East Antarctica 53 m, Greenland 7 m, West Antarctica 5 m, all mountain glaciers only ~0.4 m. Melting takes centuries to millennia.

amoc_node.caption: A toy model of the Atlantic overturning: two stable states (strong, collapsed) joined by an unstable middle branch. Past the fold (here at 0.385) the strong branch ends and the system jumps. Whether and when the real AMOC could tip is uncertain.

ozone_layer.caption: Ozone is concentrated in the stratosphere (peak near 22 km) where it absorbs harmful UV. Chlorine from CFCs destroys it, most dramatically at 14–20 km over Antarctica in spring (the ozone hole). Slide the depletion.

solar_system_formation.caption: In the young Sun's disc, temperature fell with distance. Beyond the "frost line" (~150 K, near 3 AU) ices could condense, so giants grew big cores there; inside it only rock and metal survived. A simple disc model.

planet_types.caption: Rocky planets (Mars, Earth) follow R ∝ M^0.27 and are dense; ice giants (Neptune, Uranus) are a few times bigger; gas giants (Saturn, Jupiter) stop growing in radius even as mass climbs past 300 Earth masses.

moon_origin_node.caption: The leading idea is a giant impact with a Mars-sized body (Theia), but the Moon's Earth-like isotopes are hard to explain, so variants compete.

earth_water_origin.caption: The deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio fingerprints water. Earth's oceans match carbonaceous meteorites (asteroids) better than most comets or the original solar gas, but the source is not settled. Values approximate (×10⁻⁶).

moons_tidal.caption: A moon closer than the Roche limit, d = 2.44 R·(ρ_planet/ρ_moon)^⅓, is torn apart by tides; that is where rings sit. Saturn's rings (inside ~2.3 R_S) fit the limit for icy material.

small_bodies.caption: Big impacts are rare, small ones frequent: the interval between impacts grows roughly as D^2.2. A 20 m asteroid (Chelyabinsk, 2013) arrives every few decades; a 10 km one (dinosaur-killer) every ~100 million years. Approximate.

exoplanets.caption: When a planet crosses its star the starlight dips by (R_planet/R_star)². Earth-size planets dim a Sun-like star by <0.01%; Jupiter-size ones by 1%, so big planets are easiest to find.

habitability.caption: The "habitable zone" is the band where a planet could have liquid water. Brighter, heavier stars have it farther out. Whether other conditions make a planet habitable is unknown (we have a single example). Boundaries are model-dependent.

sun_structure.caption: The Sun's layers: a core (to 0.25 R) where fusion makes energy at ~15 million K, a radiative zone where light random-walks for ~100,000 years, a convective zone of boiling plasma, and the glowing photosphere at 5800 K.

hydrostatic_balance.caption: A star is held up by a thermostat: gravity squeezes the core, raising temperature and fusion; the heat raises pressure, which pushes back. If fusion speeds up the star expands and cools, slowing fusion again (negative feedback).

stellar_spectra.caption: The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram plots luminosity against temperature. Luminosity follows L = R²(T/5772)⁴, so dashed lines are stars of equal radius. Slide a star's temperature and radius and watch it move; real stars cluster on a diagonal "main sequence". (Hot is to the right here.)

star_formation.caption: A gas cloud collapses when it exceeds the Jeans mass, M_J ∝ T^1.5/√n. Cold, dense clouds (10 K) can collapse into stars of a few solar masses; warm, thin gas cannot. Set the cloud temperature.

stellar_evolution.caption: Heavier stars burn fuel much faster: lifetime ≈ 10 billion years × (M/M☉)^−2.5. The Sun lasts ~10 Gyr; a 25 M☉ star only ~30 million years, while tiny red dwarfs outlast the current age of the universe.

stellar_death.caption: White dwarfs are supported by electron pressure, and heavier ones are smaller: radius shrinks to zero at the Chandrasekhar mass, 1.44 M☉. Beyond it the star collapses to a neutron star or black hole (often via a supernova).

nucleosynthesis_stars.caption: Abundance of elements in the Sun on a log scale (height = log₁₀ of atoms per 10¹² hydrogen). H and He came from the Big Bang; C to Fe from stars; lead and gold from rarer neutron-capture events. Sources of heavy elements are still being worked out.

kilonova_rprocess.caption: In 2017 gravitational waves and light from two merging neutron stars (GW170817) showed fresh heavy elements being made by rapid neutron capture (r-process). Mergers are one source; whether supernovae also contribute is debated.

binary_variable.caption: An eclipsing binary dims twice per orbit: once when the small star is in front (primary) and once behind. Depth ratio tells the stars' relative surface brightness. Slide the depth and temperature ratio.

distance_ladder.caption: No single method measures all distances; each rung calibrates the next. Rough maximum useful reach: parallax (Gaia) ~10 kpc, Cepheids ~30 Mpc, supernovae Ia ~1 Gpc. Small errors in the lower rungs carry up, which feeds the Hubble tension.

milky_way.caption: The Galaxy's rotation speed stays flat (~230 km/s) far from the centre, but the visible stars and gas alone (dashed) would make it fall off. A halo of unseen mass lifts it. Slide the halo strength.

galaxies.caption: Bigger galaxies spin faster: baryonic mass ∝ v⁴ (Tully–Fisher). On log axes it is a straight line, which lets astronomers estimate a galaxy's mass from its rotation speed. Slide the exponent.

dark_matter_evidence.caption: Three explanations of flat rotation curves: dark matter halo (accent), modified gravity at low acceleration (MOND, pink), or nothing (visible matter, dashed). Many observations such as cluster collisions and the CMB favour dark matter; the particle has not been found.

agn_quasars.caption: A black hole can shine no brighter than the Eddington luminosity (about 3.3×10⁴ L☉ per solar mass) or its own light would blow the gas away. Quasars are supermassive black holes feeding near that limit; Sgr A* is nearly starved. Axes are log₁₀.

smbh_growth.caption: Quasars with a billion solar masses existed less than a billion years after the Big Bang. Even steady Eddington-rate growth takes ~50 Myr per e-fold, so starting from a light seed (100 M☉) is barely fast enough; heavy seeds help. How they formed is open.

expansion_hubble.caption: Hubble's law: galaxies recede at speeds proportional to distance, v = H₀d, so the universe is expanding. Distances to galaxies and their redshift speeds fall on a line; its slope is H₀ (about 70 km/s/Mpc).

hubble_tension_node.caption: Early-universe data (CMB, BAO) give H₀ ≈ 67.4 km/s/Mpc, while the local distance ladder gives ≈ 73. The gap (~8%) is statistically large. Possible causes include measurement error or new physics; nothing is settled.

big_bang.caption: The universe was hotter in the past: the cosmic background temperature scales as T = 2.725 K × (1 + z). Light first travelled freely at ~3000 K (z ≈ 1100); nuclei formed near 10¹⁰ K, within the first minutes. Axes are log₁₀; earlier eras are extrapolations.

cmb.caption: The cosmic microwave background is the most perfect blackbody ever measured: 2.725 K, peaking near 160 GHz. It is the afterglow of the hot early universe, stretched by expansion. Slide the temperature to see how it would shift.

bbn_node.caption: Big Bang nucleosynthesis predicts how much deuterium survives: more baryons (ordinary matter) means less deuterium left. The measured D/H (2.5×10⁻⁵) fixes the baryon density, matching the CMB value (vertical line).

inflation.caption: In inflation the comoving Hubble radius shrinks, so one tiny region became everything we see and was smoothed out; afterwards it grows again. Roughly 60 e-folds of growth are needed. Inflation is a hypothesis; competing ideas exist. Vertical axis is log₁₀.

dark_energy_node.caption: Expansion is accelerating, as if driven by a "dark energy" (ΩΛ ≈ 0.7). With more of it the universe expands exponentially; with none it keeps decelerating. Its nature (a cosmological constant or something dynamic) is open. H₀ = 70 assumed.

cosmic_web.caption: A toy picture of the cosmic web: as gravity pulls matter together over time (slide g from 0 up), a smooth distribution gathers into filaments, nodes and voids, as in galaxy surveys and simulations.

reionization.caption: Ultraviolet light from the first stars and galaxies stripped electrons from the surrounding hydrogen, switching the universe from neutral to ionised between about z = 12 and 6. The exact timeline is still being measured.

fate_multiverse.caption: Possible far futures depend on dark energy: it may keep expanding (cold, empty "freeze"), eventually tear everything apart (a "rip"), or reverse and collapse (a "crunch"). Current data favour a freeze, but the future of dark energy is unknown, and ideas of other universes are untestable.

observable_universe.caption: Distance scales from the Earth to the observable universe; bar height is log₁₀ of the diameter in metres, so every step of 3 is a thousand times larger. The edge of what we can see is ~46 billion light-years away (radius), though more may lie beyond.

telescopes_tech.caption: A bigger mirror sees finer detail: the diffraction limit is θ ≈ 1.22 λ/D. Doubling the aperture halves the smallest angle; shorter wavelengths resolve more. Points mark the eye, Hubble, JWST and Keck at the chosen wavelength.

scientific_method.caption: Science is a loop: observe, form a hypothesis, derive a testable prediction, test it, and revise. Claims gain confidence as they survive repeated tests by independent groups; nothing is ever proven absolutely.

effective_theories.caption: Each level of nature has its own good description, mostly independent of the details below: chemistry does not need quark physics, biology does not need to solve the Schrödinger equation. New behaviour "emerges" at each level.

arrow_of_time.caption: Why time has a direction: the chance that N gas molecules all end up in one half of a box is 2⁻ᴺ (log₁₀ shown). For 100 molecules it is 10⁻³⁰, and for a mole it is effectively zero. Entropy rises because disordered states vastly outnumber ordered ones. Why the early universe was so ordered remains an open question.

fns.label: log₁₀ probability all in one half

information_theory.caption: Shannon entropy of a yes/no event: H = −p log₂p − (1−p) log₂(1−p). A fair coin carries 1 bit per flip; a biased coin carries less, because its outcome is more predictable.

landauer.caption: Erasing one bit must release at least kT ln 2 of heat. At room temperature this is about 3×10⁻²¹ J, far below what today's chips use (~10⁻¹⁵–10⁻¹⁷ J per operation), so there is room to improve but a real physical floor.

computation.caption: Algorithms scale differently: n², n³ remain practical, but 2ⁿ explodes: at 10⁹ operations/s, n = 60 would take years. That gap between "polynomial" and "exponential" is the heart of complexity theory.

p_vs_np.caption: P: problems solved fast. NP: problems whose answers can be checked fast. Everything in P is in NP; whether they are equal is unsolved (a $1M Millennium problem). Most experts suspect P ≠ NP (left), but no proof exists.

quantum_computing.caption: Grover's algorithm searches N items in about (π/4)√N steps instead of N/2. It is a quadratic, not exponential, speed-up; the big exponential gains (e.g. Shor's factoring) apply only to special problems. Axes are log₁₀. Useful large machines do not yet exist.

electronics_logic.caption: Digital circuits are built from gates (AND, OR, XOR…) that compute Boolean functions. This is the carry of a full adder: the output is 1 when at least two of the three bits are 1. Click the inputs.

neural_nets.caption: One artificial neuron outputs a smooth 0-to-1 value of a weighted sum of its inputs. Weights tilt the dividing line between "yes" (red) and "no" (blue); the bias shifts it. Training adjusts weights; deep networks stack many of these.

networks_complexity.caption: Many real networks (the web, airports, protein interactions) have a few hubs and many low-degree nodes: the number of nodes with degree k falls as a power law k^−γ, a straight line on log axes. Preferential attachment gives γ = 3.

fns.label: fraction of nodes with k links

readouts.label: rarity of degree-100 nodes vs degree-1

evolution_algorithm.caption: Evolution as an algorithm: copy with variation, select what works, repeat. Information about the environment accumulates in genomes over generations. The same loop drives genetic algorithms in computing.

dimensional_scaling.caption: Kleiber's law: metabolic rate scales as mass^0.75, not mass^1, across animals from mice to elephants. A straight line on log axes; an 8000-fold bigger animal needs only ~700 times the power. Slide the exponent (0.67 would follow surface-area scaling).

si_units.caption: Since 2019 all seven SI base units are defined by fixing exact values of constants of nature (left), not by physical artefacts: for example the metre via c and the kilogram via Planck's constant h.

power_grid.caption: Long-distance lines lose power as I²R, so transmitting at high voltage (low current) cuts losses: the percent loss falls as 1/V². That is why transformers step up to hundreds of kV and back down for homes.

electric_motors.caption: A DC motor's torque falls linearly with speed (stall torque at 0 rpm, none at no-load speed), so mechanical power peaks at half speed. Curves are shown as a percentage of stall torque and of peak power; readouts give real values.

batteries_tech.caption: Energy stored per kilogram: lead-acid 35, NiMH ~80, lithium-ion ~250 Wh/kg, and gasoline about 12,000 Wh/kg of chemical energy (an engine wastes ~70% of it). Batteries have improved a lot but remain far behind fuels in raw energy density.

flight_tech.caption: A wing's lift-to-drag ratio L/D rises with its aspect ratio (long, thin wings like a glider's waste less energy as wingtip vortices). Slide the aspect ratio: airliners ~9, gliders 30+.

fiber_optics.caption: Light travels through silica fibre with loss of only ~0.2 dB/km at 1550 nm, the sweet spot between scattering (falls with wavelength) and infrared absorption (rises). That low loss lets signals cross oceans with few amplifiers. A schematic of the loss curve.

readouts.label: loss over the link at 1550 nm

led_lasers.caption: An LED or laser diode emits photons with the semiconductor's band-gap energy, λ = 1240 nm·eV / E_g. Wide-gap GaN gives blue/UV; GaAs (1.42 eV) gives infrared; alloys tune the colour in between.

radio_comm.caption: Amplitude modulation: a high-frequency carrier (40 Hz here, MHz in reality) has its height varied by the message (4 Hz). The spectrum shows the carrier plus two sidebands at carrier ± message frequency.

fusion_energy.caption: Energy gain Q = fusion power out / heating power in. JET reached 0.67 (1997); the NIF laser achieved a target gain of ~1.5 in 2022 (energy out/laser energy), not counting the electricity to run the lasers; ITER aims for Q = 10 in the 2030s. Net electricity from fusion has not been shown.

plasma_physics.caption: In a plasma, charges screen each other beyond the Debye length λ_D = 7430·√(T/n) m (T in eV, n in m⁻³). Plasma behaviour needs the system to be much bigger than this. Hot, thin plasmas (solar wind) have long λ_D; dense fusion plasmas are tiny. Axes are log₁₀.

additive_manufacturing_tech.caption: Layer-by-layer printing turns a smooth 45° slope (dashed) into a staircase. Thinner layers follow the true surface better but need many more layers and more print time. Slide the layer height.

economics_basics.caption: Where the falling demand curve meets the rising supply curve, the market clears at price P* and quantity Q*. Raise demand (richer buyers) or cost of supply and the equilibrium moves; slide to see price and quantity change.

game_theory.caption: In the repeated prisoner's dilemma, cooperating (tit-for-tat) beats always defecting once the game is likely to continue long enough (probability w > (T−3)/(T−1)). Cooperation can pay when we meet again. Payoff values are standard textbook ones.

macro_economics.caption: Money grows with compound interest but loses value with inflation: after n years 100 units become 100(1+g)ⁿ (growth) or 100/(1+π)ⁿ in real terms (inflation). The rule of 70: doubling time ≈ 70 / rate%. Economic forecasts remain uncertain.

behavioral_economics.caption: Prospect theory: people feel losses about twice as strongly as equal gains (loss aversion), and feel changes with diminishing sensitivity. Slide the loss-aversion factor; the curve is steeper on the left.

readouts.label: a $50 loss feels as bad as a gain of

sociology_basics.caption: New ideas and technologies spread through a society in an S-curve (the Bass diffusion model): innovators adopt first (p), then imitation by others (q) accelerates it. Larger q gives a sharper take-off.

human_development.caption: Height at 50th percentile (typical boys and girls, approximate). Growth is fastest in infancy, slows, then spurts at puberty, earlier in girls. Development of the mind and body unfolds in these stages, with large normal variation.

language_cognition.caption: Zipf's law: in every language the r-th most common word occurs about 1/r^s times as often as the first (s ≈ 1). A few words (the, of, and) make up much of speech; most words are rare. On log axes, a straight line.

medicine_evidence.caption: Even a good test can mislead when the condition is rare: PPV = sens·p / (sens·p + (1−spec)(1−p)). With 95% sensitivity and 95% specificity, only ~16% of positives are true if prevalence is 1%. Slide prevalence and test quality.

fns.label: chance a positive test is true (%)

number_theory_crypto.caption: Arithmetic on a clock of 23 hours: each point k is joined to a·k mod 23. Simple rules produce intricate patterns (a = 2 gives a cardioid); modular arithmetic like this underlies RSA and other cryptography.

geometry_topology.caption: The Weierstrass function: a sum of ever-finer cosines that is continuous but has a rough edge at every scale (a fractal; its dimension is 2 + ln a / ln b). Slide a: small = smooth, near 1 = very jagged.

regression_models.caption: Least-squares regression picks the line that minimises the sum of squared vertical gaps between the data and the line. Adjust slope and intercept by hand and watch the error; the dashed line is the best fit.

photon_node.caption: Photoelectric effect: light ejects electrons only above a threshold frequency, however bright, with kinetic energy KE = hf − φ. This showed light comes in quanta (photons) of energy hf. Choose the metal's work function φ.

equivalence_principle.caption: Galileo's and Einstein's equivalence: in a vacuum every object falls with the same acceleration regardless of mass, because gravitational and inertial mass are equal. Change the masses: the balls still land together.

quark_gluon_plasma.caption: Map of strongly interacting matter (T vs baryon chemical potential μ_B). At low μ_B, heating changes hadrons to quark–gluon plasma smoothly near 156 MeV (~1.8 trillion K). Whether the transition becomes abrupt at higher μ_B, and where, is unknown.

superfluidity.caption: Below 2.17 K liquid helium-4 becomes a superfluid that flows without friction: a growing fraction ρₛ/ρ = 1 − (T/T_λ)^5.6 (two-fluid picture). Slide the temperature across the lambda point.

space_weather.caption: The solar wind's pressure compresses the magnetosphere: the stand-off distance falls as P^(−1/6). Normally ~10.7 Earth radii; in a strong storm it drops below geostationary orbit (6.6 R⊕), exposing satellites.

mars_node.caption: Mars compared with Earth (Earth = 1): about half the radius, a tenth of the mass, 38% of the gravity, 43% of the sunlight, but only 0.6% of the atmospheric pressure. That thin air cannot hold liquid water on the surface.

venus_node.caption: Greenhouse warming grows with the optical depth τ of the atmosphere: T = T_e (1 + 0.75τ)^¼ for a simple grey atmosphere. Earth (τ ≈ 0.8) is warmed ~33 K; Venus's thick CO₂ air (τ ≈ 130) pushes the surface to ~737 K, hotter than Mercury.

giant_planets_node.caption: The giant planets dwarf the rocky ones: Jupiter has 318 Earth masses (more than all other planets combined) and Saturn 95; Uranus and Neptune ("ice giants") ~15 and 17. Earth = 1.

shapes.text: Neptune (blue), Pluto (pink): 2 orbits of Neptune per 3 of Pluto

pluto_kuiper.caption: Pluto's orbit is tilted and elongated: it crosses inside Neptune's orbit but they never collide because Pluto circles twice for every three Neptune orbits (a 3:2 resonance). Distances in AU; animation sped up.

planet_earth_node.caption: Earth's seasons come from its 23.4° axial tilt, not from distance. Daily sunlight at a given latitude swings with the year; with no tilt there would be no seasons, and a larger tilt would make them extreme. Slide the tilt and latitude.
planet_earth_node.ylabel: mean sunlight at the top of the atmosphere (W/m²)

plant_physiology.caption: Water moves up xylem tubes by flow that scales as the radius to the fourth power (Poiseuille): a vessel twice as wide carries 16 times as much. Wide vessels transport fast but are more prone to freeze or air-bubble blockage. Relative to a 20 µm tube.

flowers_pollination.caption: Seeds and pollen land at a range of distances. Wind-spread seeds mostly fall near the parent (exponential tail); animals can carry some far away (long fat tail), which helps colonise new places. Same mean distance, different tails.

animal_diversity.caption: Described species (approximate): insects alone are about a million, outnumbering all vertebrates (~70,000) ten to one. Fungi (~150,000 described) are far more diverse than classified, with millions more estimated.

tsunami_hazards.caption: A tsunami is a shallow-water wave whose speed is √(g·depth): ~700 km/h across a 4 km-deep ocean, slowing to ~35 km/h near shore. As it slows it piles up (Green's law, height ∝ depth^−¼), growing several-fold.

enso.caption: El Niño and La Niña are irregular 2–7 year swings in Pacific sea-surface temperature. Positive anomalies above about +0.5 °C mean El Niño. This is an idealised oscillation; the real one is irregular and only partly predictable. Slide the period.

biomes_climate.caption: Climate (temperature and rainfall) largely decides which biome grows: cold = tundra/boreal forest, wet and warm = rainforest, dry = desert or grassland. A rough sketch of the Whittaker diagram; drag the climate point.

fossils_paleontology.caption: Radiocarbon dating works only for recent remains: carbon-14 (half-life 5730 yr) fades below measurable levels after ~50,000 years. Older fossils are dated from radioactive minerals in the surrounding volcanic rocks.

energy_systems.caption: Where the world's primary energy comes from (share, about 2022, approximate): fossil fuels still supply roughly 80%. Hydro, nuclear and wind/solar/other renewables fill most of the rest. Shares are changing as renewables grow.

demography_agriculture.caption: World population took all of history to reach 1 billion (about 1800), then added the next billions ever faster, helped by agriculture and the Haber–Bosch fertiliser. Growth is now slowing; the 2050 value is a UN projection and uncertain.

symmetry_conservation_summary.caption: Each continuous symmetry matches a conserved quantity (Noether). Symmetries that are only approximate or broken (like parity in the weak force) give quantities that are not always conserved.

string_theory_holography.caption: String theory replaces point particles with tiny vibrating strings, and the AdS/CFT duality says a gravity theory in a volume equals a quantum theory without gravity on its boundary. Both are mathematically rich, but untested by experiment.

loop_quantum_gravity.caption: In loop quantum gravity space is a network of discrete links (a "spin network"): area and volume come in indivisible units of order the Planck scale. One of several candidates for quantum gravity (with strings, causal sets and others); none is confirmed.

machine_consciousness.caption: Whether a machine could be conscious depends on what consciousness is, which is unsettled. Views differ: computation might suffice, hardware might matter, or life itself might be required. No test exists.
